name: Hair bangs / frame hairstyle for eyes
lead: Bangs (called a fringe in British, Australian and New Zealand English) are strands of hair that fall over the forehead, usually just above the eyebrows. In looksmaxxing and styling discussions, bangs and other face-framing cuts are used to put the focus on the eyes and brow, shorten the look of a tall forehead, and soften or hide a hairline.[1][2][3]

The style is old and varied. Blunt, curtain, choppy, feathered and see-through fringes each frame the upper face differently, and fringes appear in the records of ancient Egypt, Greece and Rome as well as in Victorian and modern fashion.[1]

Formal research on how bangs change the way eyes or faces are perceived is thin. A 2022 cosmetology paper by Park and Jang paired five hairline shapes with fringe styles using wig prototypes, and the study states that hair makes up most of a person's perceived appearance.[1]

angle.text: A fringe changes what the upper third of the face looks like straight away: it can hide a long forehead or thinning hairline and place a line of hair just above the brows. Forum users describe wearing a messy or wavy fringe as a way to look younger and more eye-centered.

infobox: Over the forehead, around eyebrow level[1]
Blunt, curtain, choppy, feather, heart, see-through[1]

paras: Wikipedia lists blunt (straight-cut) bangs, the short frizzy Alexandra fringe, the mop-top, curtain bangs that part in the middle and frame the face, and choppy, heart, feather and see-through styles.[1]

The 2022 Park and Jang study classifies five hairline shapes (round, heart, angular, triangular and flat) and pairs each with a fringe: choppy for round, heart bangs for heart, feather for angular, blunt for triangular and see-through for flat. The authors intend the pairings as educational material for cosmetology and styling.[1]

Fringes appear in ancient Egypt, Greece and Rome and in medieval art. In the 1600s clergy warned that they signaled vanity, and curled bangs returned in the Victorian era, with the Alexandra fringe popular in the 1880s.[1]

Wikipedia notes that in the late 19th and early 20th century young immigrant women in the US wore bangs to cover blemishes such as acne and smallpox scars. Bangs were uncommon among men until British bands such as the Beatles popularized them from about 1963. A thick blunt revival began in 2007, and curtain bangs trended in the 2020s, partly through TikTok.[1]

Threads on looksmax.org argue that a fringe suits almost everyone, with one poster naming male models he thinks look best in it and others calling it a way to cover a receding hairline.[2][3][4] Members also trade product and cut advice for wavy and messy fringes, and share a thread pointing to a model's fringe as a template.[5][6]
One member described asking a stylist for a messy fringe and finding afterward that it needed products to hold, illustrating that the look depends on cut, texture and styling.[7]
No studies found on bangs and eye attractiveness. The nearest published work is the 2022 cosmetology paper pairing hairlines with fringe styles, which relied on wig prototypes.[1]

timeline.event: The Alexandra fringe becomes popular in Victorian fashion.[1]
British bands led by the Beatles begin popularising bangs among men.[1]
A revival of thick blunt-cut bangs begins.[1]
Curtain bangs resurge, partly through TikTok.[1]

lore.intro: Fringes are a frequent hairstyle topic on looksmax.org, where members treat them as a flattering default and a way to manage hairline.[2][3][4]

claims.claim: A fringe flatters almost any face
claims.believers: A poster says there is no reason to wear another style and points to models who look best in a fringe.[2]
claims.experts: No published studies have tested this. The 2022 cosmetology paper suggests different fringe types suit different hairline shapes rather than one style fitting all.[1]

claims.claim: A fringe hides a receding hairline
claims.believers: Posters say it covers a reduced hairline, with one advising early recession to wear a fringe.[3][4]
claims.experts: Bangs cover the forehead by definition, and Wikipedia records that historically people wore them to cover blemishes.[1]

card.summary: Fringe and face-framing hair used to draw attention to the eyes and brow area; a styling choice with little formal research behind the claims.
card.note: Evidence is limited to a cosmetology paper pairing hairlines with fringe styles.

quick.overview:
Bangs (fringe in British usage) are hair that falls over the front hairline to cover the forehead, usually just above the eyebrows. In looksmaxxing discussions, bangs and face-framing styles are said to focus attention on the eye and brow area and to alter the apparent forehead and face shape.

Bangs have a long history across cultures and fashions. Formal research on their effect on eye attractiveness is sparse.
quick.mechanism: Hair covering the forehead changes the visible hairline and frames the upper face. Proponents say this shifts attention to the eyes and shortens a long forehead. A 2022 cosmetology paper cited by Wikipedia paired five hairline shapes with fringe styles.
quick.risks: Styling carries no significant health risks. Practitioners note that bangs need regular trimming and styling.
